Ecclesiastes — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)

The title Ecclesiastes means “The Preacher.”

Here God's wisdom preaches to us through Solomon, whom Henry identifies as the author.

Henry presents the book as a record written by Solomon near the end of his life, when he had come to understand his own sin and foolishness.

Solomon described his experience for the benefit of others; Henry calls the book the record of his repentance.

His conclusion concerning earthly goods was that they are all vanity and vexation of spirit.

This book teaches the emptiness of the world and its inability to make us happy. It also exposes sin's evil and the misery toward which sin inevitably leads.

No created good can finally satisfy the soul.

True happiness is found in God alone.

Through the teaching of the blessed Holy Spirit, this truth must lead the heart to Jesus Christ.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesSolomon shows that all human things are vain.1–3Man's toil and want of satisfaction.4–8There is nothing new.9–11The vexation in pursuit of knowledge.12–18
Solomon declares the world's vanity (verses 1–3)

We can learn a great deal by comparing one part of Scripture with another.

Here we see Solomon returning from the world's broken and empty cisterns to the Fountain of living water.

He records the foolishness and shame of his former choices, the bitterness of disappointment and the lessons he learned.

People who have themselves been warned and have turned away from death should warn others not to continue toward destruction.

Solomon does not merely say that worldly things are vain. He says they are vanity itself.

“Vanity of vanities! All is vanity!”

This is the central theme of the Preacher's message, and he never loses sight of it throughout this book.

If life in this fallen world were all we could look forward to, living for it would be futile.

Even the greatest abundance of wealth and pleasure cannot make a human being happy.

What do we gain from all our work?

We cannot use its profits to meet the soul's needs, satisfy its desires, atone for its sins or prevent its destruction.

What will worldly wealth profit the soul at death, in judgment or in eternity?

Human work never finally satisfies (verses 4–8)

Everything changes, and nothing remains at rest.

Despite all human effort, people are no nearer to finding true rest than the sun, the wind or the flowing river.

Our souls will find no lasting rest unless it comes from God.

Our bodily senses soon grow weary of what they experience, yet they still long for something new and untried.

Nothing is truly new (verses 9–11)

Human hearts are still marked by the same fallen corruption as in earlier generations.

Their desires, pursuits and complaints have not fundamentally changed.

Recognizing this should lead us to stop expecting happiness from created things and to seek eternal blessings instead.

How many people and accomplishments were celebrated as extraordinary in Solomon's time, yet no one remembers them now?

Even great knowledge leaves the soul unsatisfied (verses 12–18)

Solomon examined every kind of pursuit and found vanity.

Even his studies and investigations into knowledge wearied him, not only physically but mentally.

The more deeply he considered what happens under the sun, the more clearly he saw its emptiness, and the more troubled he became.

He could neither gain the satisfaction he hoped for nor accomplish as much good for others as he had imagined.

Pursuing wisdom and knowledge exposed human wickedness and misery.

The more Solomon learned, the more reason he saw for sorrow.

Let us therefore hate and fear sin, the cause of the world's emptiness and misery.

Let us value Christ and seek our rest in knowing, loving and serving the Savior.
classic_reading:
[Eccl.1.1-Eccl.1.3]
Ecclesiastes
The name of this book signifies "The Preacher." The wisdom of God here preaches to us, speaking by Solomon, who it is evident was the author. At the close of his life, being made sensible of his sin and folly, he recorded here his experience for the benefit of others, as the book of his repentance; and he pronounced all earthly good to be "vanity and vexation of spirit." It convinces us of the vanity of the world, and that it cannot make us happy; of the vileness of sin, and its certain tendency to make us miserable. It shows that no created good can satisfy the soul, and that happiness is to be found in God alone; and this doctrine must, under the blessed Spirit's teaching, lead the heart to Christ Jesus.
Chapter 1
Solomon shows that all human things are vain. (Eccl. 1:1-3) Man's toil and want of satisfaction. (Eccl. 1:4-8) There is nothing new. (Eccl. 1:9-11) The vexation in pursuit of knowledge. (Eccl. 1:12-18)
Verses 1-3 Much is to be learned by comparing one part of Scripture with another. We here behold Solomon returning from the broken and empty cisterns of the world, to the Fountain of living water; recording his own folly and shame, the bitterness of his disappointment, and the lessons he had learned. Those that have taken warning to turn and live, should warn others not to go on and die. He does not merely say all things are vain, but that they are vanity. VANITY OF VANITIES, ALL IS VANITY. This is the text of the preacher's sermon, of which in this book he never loses sight. If this world, in its present state, were all, it would not be worth living for; and the wealth and pleasure of this world, if we had ever so much, are not enough to make us happy. What profit has a man of all his labour? All he gets by it will not supply the wants of the soul, nor satisfy its desires; will not atone for the sins of the soul, nor hinder the loss of it: what profit will the wealth of the world be to the soul in death, in judgment, or in the everlasting state?
[Eccl.1.4-Eccl.1.8]
Verses 4-8 All things change, and never rest. Man, after all his labour, is no nearer finding rest than the sun, the wind, or the current of the river. His soul will find no rest, if he has it not from God. The senses are soon tired, yet still craving what is untried.
[Eccl.1.9-Eccl.1.11]
Verses 9-11 Men's hearts and their corruptions are the same now as in former times; their desires, and pursuits, and complaints, still the same. This should take us from expecting happiness in the creature, and quicken us to seek eternal blessings. How many things and persons in Solomon's day were thought very great, yet there is no remembrance of them now!
[Eccl.1.12-Eccl.1.18]
Verses 12-18 Solomon tried all things, and found them vanity. He found his searches after knowledge weariness, not only to the flesh, but to the mind. The more he saw of the works done under the sun, the more he saw their vanity; and the sight often vexed his spirit. He could neither gain that satisfaction to himself, nor do that good to others, which he expected. Even the pursuit of knowledge and wisdom discovered man's wickedness and misery; so that the more he knew, the more he saw cause to lament and mourn. Let us learn to hate and fear sin, the cause of all this vanity and misery; to value Christ; to seek rest in the knowledge, love, and service of the Saviour.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe vanity and vexation of mirth, sensual pleasure, riches, and pomp.1–11Human wisdom insufficient.12–17This world to be used according to the will of God.18–26
Pleasure, wealth and magnificence cannot satisfy (verses 1–11)

Solomon soon discovered that laughter and pleasure were vanity.

Loud, glittering entertainment does little to make a person genuinely happy.

The many things people attempt in order to find satisfaction in the world—and the way they keep moving from one to another—resemble a feverish person's restless tossing.

When Solomon realized the folly of giving himself to wine, he turned to the expensive amusements and entertainments of rulers.

Poor people reading the description may be tempted to envy him or resent their own circumstances.

But the remedy is to listen to the wealthy man's own judgment on those pleasures.

They were all vanity and vexation of spirit.

The same experiences would bring us the same disappointing result.

Having food and clothing, let us learn to be content.

Solomon retained his great human knowledge and understanding throughout these experiments.

Yet worldly pleasure, when separated from spiritual blessings, leaves the mind still longing for more and never truly satisfied.

Happiness does not come from the social position or circumstances we occupy.

Final blessedness comes only through Jesus Christ.

Human wisdom cannot make a person finally happy (verses 12–17)

Solomon found that knowledge and prudence are better than ignorance and foolishness.

Nevertheless, human learning and wisdom cannot give eternal happiness.

The greatest scholar who dies without knowing Jesus Christ is lost just as surely as the person who never received an education.

What value will worldly praise have for the body in the grave or the soul in hell?

And those whose spirits have been made perfect in heaven have no need of it either.

If this world were all we had, these things might cause us to despair of earthly life as nothing but vanity and vexation of spirit.

Use this world's gifts according to God's will (verses 18–26)

Our hearts are often reluctant to give up their expectation of finding something truly great and lasting in the created world.

Solomon eventually learned to surrender that expectation.

Even wealthy people live in a valley of tears.

It is foolish to become a slave to worldly pursuits when they can provide nothing greater than support for the body.

At best we can enjoy a moderate and cheerful use of earthly things, suited to our circumstances and position.

But we should also take joy in honest work.

The things God gives us should help us fulfill our ordinary responsibilities diligently and cheerfully.

This contentment is God's gift.

Wealth can be either a blessing or a curse, depending on whether a person has a heart that uses it wisely.

God gives those he accepts joy and satisfaction in knowing and loving him.

But sinners who make the world their entire portion find labor, sorrow, emptiness and vexation—then ultimately leave the wealth they pursued to other people.

Let sinners reflect seriously upon their end.

Seeking a lasting inheritance in Christ's love and the blessings that follow from it is the only way to enjoy even present life in a truly satisfying way.
classic_reading:
[Eccl.2.1-Eccl.2.11]
Chapter 2
The vanity and vexation of mirth, sensual pleasure, riches, and pomp. (Eccl. 2:1-11) Human wisdom insufficient. (Eccl. 2:12-17) This world to be used according to the will of God. (Eccl. 2:18-26)
Verses 1-11 Solomon soon found mirth and pleasure to be vanity. What does noisy, flashy mirth towards making a man happy? The manifold devices of men's hearts, to get satisfaction from the world, and their changing from one thing to another, are like the restlessness of a man in a fever. Perceiving it was folly to give himself to wine, he next tried the costly amusements of princes. The poor, when they read such a description, are ready to feel discontent. But the remedy against all such feelings is in the estimate of it all by the owner himself. All was vanity and vexation of spirit: and the same things would yield the same result to us, as to Solomon. Having food and raiment, let us therewith be content. His wisdom remained with him; a strong understanding, with great human knowledge. But every earthly pleasure, when unconnected with better blessings, leaves the mind as eager and unsatisfied as before. Happiness arises not from the situation in which we are placed. It is only through Jesus Christ that final blessedness can be attained.
[Eccl.2.12-Eccl.2.17]
Verses 12-17 Solomon found that knowledge and prudence were preferable to ignorance and folly, though human wisdom and knowledge will not make a man happy. The most learned of men, who dies a stranger to Christ Jesus, will perish equally with the most ignorant; and what good can commendations on earth do to the body in the grave, or the soul in hell? And the spirits of just men made perfect cannot want them. So that if this were all, we might be led to hate our life, as it is all vanity and vexation of spirit.
[Eccl.2.18-Eccl.2.26]
Verses 18-26 Our hearts are very loth to quit their expectations of great things from the creature; but Solomon came to this at length. The world is a vale of tears, even to those that have much of it. See what fools they are, who make themselves drudges to the world, which affords a man nothing better than subsistence for the body. And the utmost he can attain in this respect is to allow himself a sober, cheerful use thereof, according to his rank and condition. But we must enjoy good in our labour; we must use those things to make us diligent and cheerful in worldly business. And this is the gift of God. Riches are a blessing or a curse to a man, according as he has, or has not, a heart to make a good use of them. To those that are accepted of the Lord, he gives joy and satisfaction in the knowledge and love of him. But to the sinner he allots labour, sorrow, vanity, and vexation, in seeking a worldly portion, which yet afterwards comes into better hands. Let the sinner seriously consider his latter end. To seek a lasting portion in the love of Christ and the blessings it bestows, is the only way to true and satisfying enjoyment even of this present world.

The changing seasons of human life (verses 1–10)

Anyone seeking lasting happiness in an ever-changing world will be disappointed.

It is our duty and wisdom to accept the circumstances God appoints and live faithfully in them.

His whole plan for governing the world will eventually prove wise, just and good.

We should therefore seize favorable opportunities for every good purpose and task.

The time when we must die is coming quickly.

Meanwhile human life is full of labor and sorrow.

Yet God allows us to experience this work so that we always have something useful to do.

No one was sent into the world merely to be idle.

God's purposes do not change (verses 11–15)

Things truly are as God has made them, not necessarily as they appear to us.

Worldly concerns so fill our hearts and minds that we often lack the time or desire to notice God's hand in events.

The world not only takes possession of our affections; it also leads us to form unfair thoughts about the beauty of God's works.

We are mistaken if we think we were born only for ourselves.

Our task is to do good during a brief and uncertain life.

Because our time for such service is limited, we must use it carefully.

Being content with God's Providence means trusting that all things work together for good for those who love him.

God acts so that people will reverence him.

As the world has been, so it is now and so it will be.

Every change and temptation we meet belongs to the kinds of experiences shared by humanity.

We are not enduring some entirely unprecedented form of testing.

Worldly power cannot escape final judgment (verses 16–22)

Without reverence for the Lord, human authority is empty.

When judges cast aside fear of God, they misuse their power.

But another Judge stands at the door.

God has appointed a time to correct injustices, even if we do not yet see that correction.

Solomon appears to wish that people would recognize this: by choosing the present world as their ultimate portion, they bring their lives down toward the level of animals, while still enduring the anxieties of this life and awaiting an account of their conduct.

Both humans and animals return to the dust from which they were taken.

How little reason we have to boast about our bodies or physical accomplishments!

But the human rational soul and an animal's life are fundamentally different, even if few people think properly about the difference.

Henry explains that the human spirit goes upward to judgment, where its eternal state is fixed in unchanging happiness or misery.

The life of an animal, by contrast, perishes with the animal's death.

How pitiable are those whose greatest wish is simply to die as animals die!

Our crucial question is how eternal existence may become eternal happiness.

That is the great purpose of revelation.

Jesus is revealed as the Son of God and the Hope of sinners.
classic_reading:
[Eccl.3.1-Eccl.3.10]
Chapter 3
The changes of human affairs. (Eccl. 3:1-10) The Divine counsels unchangeable. (Eccl. 3:11-15) The vanity of worldly power. (Eccl. 3:16-22)
Verses 1-10 To expect unchanging happiness in a changing world, must end in disappointment. To bring ourselves to our state in life, is our duty and wisdom in this world. God's whole plan for the government of the world will be found altogether wise, just, and good. Then let us seize the favourable opportunity for every good purpose and work. The time to die is fast approaching. Thus labour and sorrow fill the world. This is given us, that we may always have something to do; none were sent into the world to be idle.
[Eccl.3.11-Eccl.3.15]
Verses 11-15 Every thing is as God made it; not as it appears to us. We have the world so much in our hearts, are so taken up with thoughts and cares of worldly things, that we have neither time nor spirit to see God's hand in them. The world has not only gained possession of the heart, but has formed thoughts against the beauty of God's works. We mistake if we think we were born for ourselves; no, it is our business to do good in this life, which is short and uncertain; we have but little time to be doing good, therefore we should redeem time. Satisfaction with Divine Providence, is having faith that all things work together for good to them that love him. God doeth all, that men should fear before him. The world, as it has been, is, and will be. There has no change befallen us, nor has any temptation by it taken us, but such as is common to men.
[Eccl.3.16-Eccl.3.22]
Verses 16-22 Without the fear of the Lord, man is but vanity; set that aside, and judges will not use their power well. And there is another Judge that stands before the door. With God there is a time for the redressing of grievances, though as yet we see it not. Solomon seems to express his wish that men might perceive, that by choosing this world as their portion, they brought themselves to a level with the beasts, without being free, as they are, from present vexations and a future account. Both return to the dust from whence they were taken. What little reason have we to be proud of our bodies, or bodily accomplishments! But as none can fully comprehend, so few consider properly, the difference between the rational soul of man, and the spirit or life of the beast. The spirit of man goes upward, to be judged, and is then fixed in an unchangeable state of happiness or misery. It is as certain that the spirit of the beast goes downward to the earth; it perishes at death. Surely their case is lamentable, the height of whose hopes and wishes is, that they may die like beasts. Let our inquiry be, how an eternity of existence may be to us an eternity of enjoyment? To answer this, is the grand design of revelation. Jesus is revealed as the Son of God, and the Hope of sinners.

The misery caused by oppression (verses 1–3)

Solomon grieved when he saw power overcoming justice.

Wherever we look, we see sorrowful evidence of human wickedness and misery.

People create suffering both for themselves and for one another.

Those treated cruelly may become so miserable that they wish they had never been born.

But a godly person, though suffering in this life, has no true reason to make that wish.

Such a person may be glorifying the Lord even in the fire and will ultimately enjoy everlasting happiness.

The ungodly have still greater reason to desire that their present lives continue, despite their troubles, because if they die unrepentant their future condition will be far worse.

If earthly and human things were the highest possible good, then given all the world's oppression, not existing would be preferable.

But they are not the highest good.

Envy and indolence both cause trouble (verses 4–6)

Those who work diligently and succeed often attract envy and opposition.

Other people, seeing the difficulties and hostility faced by hardworking neighbors, imagine they would find greater happiness in doing nothing.

But idleness is a sin that brings its own punishment.

Let us earn enough through honest work to obtain our necessities—the metaphorical one handful—rather than grasping for two overflowing handfuls and filling our lives with anxiety.

Moderate effort and moderate gain are best.

Selfish greed cannot be satisfied (verses 7 and 8)

Often the more people possess, the more they desire.

They become so absorbed in accumulating wealth that they cannot enjoy what they already own.

Selfishness lies at the heart of this folly.

Such people care for almost no one—not even enough for themselves to allow sufficient rest for themselves or their workers.

They may have everything necessary for their employment and family but still feel that their eyes have not seen enough.

Worldliness can rob people not only of God's favor and eternal life but also of this life's ordinary pleasures.

Relatives or strangers may inherit the fortune they accumulated, yet will feel no gratitude for the sacrifice.

Greed grows with practice and advancing age, sometimes becoming strongest when the grave is near.

How astonishing that people claiming to follow Christ, who became poor for our sake though he was rich, can still obsessively hoard money while excusing themselves through talk of prudent provision and the dangers of extravagance!

Mutual assistance and fellowship (verses 9–12)

Someone working hard to support loved ones gains more satisfaction than a miser laboring only to accumulate money.

Cooperation makes many things safer and more effective.

This is especially true of fellowship between Christians.

Believers strengthen one another through encouragement and friendly correction.

They warm one another's hearts by speaking of Christ's love and singing his praise together.

Let us use our opportunities for Christian friendship well.

Not everything in such fellowship is vanity, although its joys remain imperfect in this life.

When two people unite in holy love and fellowship, Christ by his Spirit joins them, forming a threefold cord.

Even royal favor changes (verses 13–16)

People are rarely satisfied for long.

They become eager for change and easily grow tired of their rulers.

That is nothing new.

Kings can find themselves rejected by people they made great efforts to help.

Such is the emptiness and frustration of worldly honor.

But the willing servants of our King, the Lord Jesus, rejoice in him alone, and their love for him will grow forever.
classic_reading:
[Eccl.4.1-Eccl.4.3]
Chapter 4
Miseries from oppression. (Eccl. 4:1-3) troubles from envy. (Eccl. 4:4-6) The folly of covetousness. (Eccl. 4:7,8) The advantages of mutual assistance. (Eccl. 4:9-12) the changes of royalty. (Eccl. 4:13-16)
Verses 1-3 It grieved Solomon to see might prevail against right. Wherever we turn, we see melancholy proofs of the wickedness and misery of mankind, who try to create trouble to themselves and to each other. Being thus hardly used, men are tempted to hate and despise life. But a good man, though badly off while in this world, cannot have cause to wish he had never been born, since he is glorifying the Lord, even in the fires, and will be happy at last, for ever happy. Ungodly men have most cause to wish the continuance of life with all its vexations, as a far more miserable condition awaits them if they die in their sins. If human and worldly things were our chief good, not to exist would be preferable to life, considering the various oppressions here below.
[Eccl.4.4-Eccl.4.6]
Verses 4-6 Solomon notices the sources of trouble peculiar to well-doers, and includes all who labour with diligence, and whose efforts are crowned with success. They often become great and prosperous, but this excites envy and opposition. Others, seeing the vexations of an active course, foolishly expect more satisfaction in sloth and idleness. But idleness is a sin that is its own punishment. Let us by honest industry lay hold on the handful, that we may not want necessaries, but not grasp at both hands full, which would only create vexation of spirit. Moderate pains and gains do best.
[Eccl.4.7-Eccl.4.8]
Verse 7 ,8 Frequently, the more men have, the more they would have; and on this they are so intent, that they get no enjoyment from what they have. Selfishness is the cause of this evil. A selfish man cares for nobody; there is none to take care of but himself, yet he will scarcely allow necessary rest to himself, and the people he employs. He never thinks he has enough. He has enough for his calling, for his family, but he has not enough for his eyes. Many are so set upon the world, that in pursuit of it they bereave themselves, not only of the favour of God and eternal life, but of the pleasures of this life. The distant relations or strangers who inherit such a man's wealth, never thank him. Covetousness gathers strength by time and habit; men tottering on the brink of the grave, grow more grasping and griping. Alas, and how often do we see men professing to be followers of Him, who, "though he was rich, for our sakes became poor," anxiously scraping money together and holding it fast, excusing themselves by common-place talking about the necessity of care, and the danger of extravagance!
[Eccl.4.9-Eccl.4.12]
Verses 9-12 Surely he has more satisfaction in life, who labours hard to maintain those he loves, than the miser has in his toil. In all things union tends to success and safety, but above all, the union of Christians. They assist each other by encouragement, or friendly reproof. They warm each other's hearts while they converse together of the love of Christ, or join in singing his praises. Then let us improve our opportunities of Christian fellowship. In these things all is not vanity, though there will be some alloy as long as we are under the sun. Where two are closely joined in holy love and fellowship, Christ will by his Spirit come to them; then there is a threefold cord.
[Eccl.4.13-Eccl.4.16]
Verses 13-16 People are never long easy and satisfied; they are fond of changes. This is no new thing. Princes see themselves slighted by those they have studied to oblige; this is vanity and vexation of spirit. But the willing servants of the Lord Jesus, our King, rejoice in him alone, and they will love Him more and more to all eternity.

Worship, words and wandering thoughts (verses 1–3)

When approaching God in worship, take time to prepare your mind.

Guard your thoughts against wandering, and keep your affections from becoming absorbed in wrong things.

We should avoid meaningless repetition.

The passage does not condemn long or detailed prayers in themselves.

It condemns prayers made up of words that carry no sincere meaning.

Our thoughts wander so frequently that attendance at God's appointed worship can become little better than the sacrifice of fools.

Hasty and thoughtless words in prayer reveal a foolish heart, a low view of God and carelessness concerning our souls.

Vows, fear of people and injustice (verses 4–8)

When people make promises rashly, their own words lead them into sin.

Henry describes a person coming before the priest and trying to excuse a vow by claiming it was rash or wrong to fulfill.

Such mockery of God could bring his displeasure and destroy the gain the person hoped to retain improperly.

Do not be controlled by fear of other people.

Keep God before your eyes.

When you see the poor oppressed, do not use that wrongdoing to accuse divine Providence of injustice.

Nor should you despise the institution of civil government merely because people corrupt its purposes.

Likewise, do not reject religion because faithful people sometimes suffer mistreatment.

Even if oppressors seem secure for a long time, God will call everyone to account.

The vanity of great riches (verses 9–17)

The kindness of God's Providence is distributed more widely than a careless observer may imagine.

A king needs the same basic necessities of life as other people.

Poor people may enjoy simple food more than a king enjoys a luxurious feast.

Certain bodily needs cannot be satisfied by silver, and worldly abundance cannot satisfy the soul's spiritual desires.

More wealth requires a bigger household, more servants, more guests and more people depending upon it.

A laborer often sleeps well, not only because of physical tiredness, but because there are few anxious responsibilities to interrupt the night.

The believer who has worked diligently in God's service can also rest sweetly in him, even in the long sleep of death.

By contrast, people who possess almost everything may still be unable to obtain a good night's sleep.

Their abundance itself becomes the source of anxiety.

Riches can harm their owners, leading the heart away from God and duty.

Rich people may also use wealth to indulge their own sinful desires and oppress others.

At death they discover that their work was labor for the wind.

They cannot tell where the benefits have gone.

When worldly people lose what they coveted, they often respond not with godly repentance but by anger toward God's Providence and everyone around them, multiplying their misery.

Enjoy God's gifts with grateful obedience (verses 18–20)

Life is God's gift.

We should not regard our vocation as mere drudgery but seek appropriate joy in the work God has assigned us.

A cheerful spirit is a great gift.

It makes duties easier and suffering more bearable.

Those who have used wealth rightly may remember earlier days with thankfulness and comfort.

Solomon repeatedly describes God as the Giver of both life and its enjoyment.

We must therefore receive his gifts and use them according to his will and for his glory.

Let this passage lead us to Christ's gracious command:

Do not labor only for food that perishes, but for food enduring to eternal life.

Christ is the Bread of Life, the soul's only true food.

Everyone is invited to receive this heavenly provision.
classic_reading:
[Eccl.5.1-Eccl.5.3]
Chapter 5
What renders devotion vain. (Eccl. 5:1-3) Of vows, and oppression. (Eccl. 5:4-8) the vanity of riches shown. (Eccl. 5:9-7) The right use of riches. (Eccl. 5:18-20)
Verses 1-3 Address thyself to the worship of God, and take time to compose thyself for it. Keep thy thoughts from roving and wandering: keep thy affections from running out toward wrong objects. We should avoid vain repetitions; copious prayers are not here condemned, but those that are unmeaning. How often our wandering thoughts render attendance on Divine ordinances little better than the sacrifice of fools! Many words and hasty ones, used in prayer, show folly in the heart, low thoughts of God, and careless thoughts of our own souls.
[Eccl.5.4-Eccl.5.8]
Verses 4-8 When a person made engagements rashly, he suffered his mouth to cause his flesh to sin. The case supposes a man coming to the priest, and pretending that his vow was made rashly, and that it would be wrong to fulfil it. Such mockery of God would bring the Divine displeasure, which might blast what was thus unduly kept. We are to keep down the fear of man. Set God before thee; then, if thou seest the oppression of the poor, thou wilt not find fault with Divine Providence; nor think the worse of the institution of magistracy, when thou seest the ends of it thus perverted; nor of religion, when thou seest it will not secure men from suffering wrong. But though oppressors may be secure, God will reckon for all.
[Eccl.5.9-Eccl.5.17]
Verses 9-17 The goodness of Providence is more equally distributed than appears to a careless observer. The king needs the common things of life, and the poor share them; they relish their morsel better than he does his luxuries. There are bodily desires which silver itself will not satisfy, much less will worldly abundance satisfy spiritual desires. The more men have, the better house they must keep, the more servants they must employ, the more guests they must entertain, and the more they will have hanging on them. The sleep of the labourer is sweet, not only because he is tired, but because he has little care to break his sleep. The sleep of the diligent Christian, and his long sleep, are sweet; having spent himself and his time in the service of God, he can cheerfully repose in God as his Rest. But those who have every thing else, often fail to secure a good night's sleep; their abundance breaks their rest. Riches do hurt, and draw away the heart from God and duty. [Eccl.7.11-Eccl.7.22]
Verses 11-22 Wisdom is as good as an inheritance, yea better. It shelters from the storms and scorching heat of trouble. Wealth will not lengthen out the natural life; but true wisdom will give spiritual life, and strengthen men for services under their sufferings. Let us look upon the disposal of our condition as the work of God, and at last all will appear to have been for the best. In acts of righteousness, be not carried into heats or passions, no, not by a zeal for God. Be not conceited of thine own abilities; nor find fault with every thing, nor busy thyself in other men's matters. Many who will not be wrought upon by the fear of God, and the dread of hell, will avoid sins which ruin their health and estate, and expose to public justice. But those that truly fear God, have but one end to serve, therefore act steadily. If we say we have not sinned, we deceive ourselves. Every true believer is ready to say, God be merciful to me a sinner. Forget not at the same time, that personal righteousness, walking in newness of life, is the only real evidence of an interest by faith in the righteousness of the Redeemer. Wisdom teaches us not to be quick in resenting affronts. Be not desirous to know what people say; if they speak well of thee, it will feed thy pride, if ill, it will stir up thy passion. He alone who constantly aims to please God, can expect to escape; the careless sinner probably will fall to rise no more. He now discovered more than ever the evil of the great sin of which he had been guilty, the loving many strange women, I Kin. 11:1. A woman thoroughly upright and godly, he had not found. How was he likely to find such a one among those he had collected? If any of them had been well disposed, their situation would tend to render them all nearly of the same character. He here warns others against the sins into which he had been betrayed. Many a godly man can with thankfulness acknowledge that he has found a prudent, virtuous woman in the wife of his bosom; but those men who have gone in Solomon's track, cannot expect to find one. He traces up all the streams of actual transgression to the fountain. It is clear that man is corrupted and revolted, and not as he was made. It is lamentable that man, whom God made upright, has found out so many ways to render himself wicked and miserable. Let us bless Him for Jesus Christ, and seek his grace, that we may be numbered with his chosen people.

But sinful folly makes men miss that only way to happiness.
[Eccl.10.16-Eccl.10.20]
Verses 16-20 The happiness of a land depends on the character of its rulers. The people cannot be happy when their princes are childish, and lovers of pleasure. Slothfulness is of ill consequence both to private and public affairs. Money, of itself, will neither feed nor clothe, though it answers the occasions of this present life, as what is to be had, may generally be had for money. But the soul, as it is not redeemed, so it is not maintained with corruptible things, as silver and gold. God sees what men do, and hears what they say in secret; and, when he pleases, brings it to light by strange and unsuspected ways. If there be hazard in secret thoughts and whispers against earthly rulers, what must be the peril from every deed, word, or thought of rebellion against the King of kings, and Lord of lords! He seeth in secret. His ear is ever open. Sinner! curse not THIS KING in thy inmost thought. Your curses cannot affect Him; but his curse, coming down upon you, will sink you to the lowest hell.
